title: The sentence of death (2 Corinthians 1:8–11)
hookLine: Paul despaired even of life, and learned to trust the God who raises the dead
tomorrow: how can one smell mean life to one person and death to another?

lines: A PLASTIC CHAIR, A HUMMING MACHINE.
cards: A hospital hallway. A plastic chair, a vending machine humming, a door that hasn't opened in an hour. You've already run the worst version in your head three times.
Paul put a season like that into a letter. "We were pressed out of measure, above strength, insomuch that we despaired even of life." He names the place, Asia, and stops there.
He never says what happened. Then he says something stranger: he'd already heard the verdict.

teach.h: THE SENTENCE OF DEATH IN OURSELVES.
teach.b: Here it is: "But we had the sentence of death in ourselves, that we should not trust in ourselves, but in God which raiseth the dead." A sentence, like a verdict read out in court. Paul felt it was already in.
And he says the verdict did something: it moved his trust off himself.
Notice which name for God he reaches for. Not the God who helps the strong get stronger. The God who raises the dead.
When you're at the bottom, that's the help that reaches that far down. Then three tenses in one breath.
God "delivered us from so great a death, and doth deliver: in whom we trust that he will yet deliver us." Past, present, future.
Then Paul pulls the readers into it: "Ye also helping together by prayer for us."
Their prayers, he says, are part of how he's carried, and many will give thanks when he comes through.

One to tell a friend tonight: a few verses earlier Paul calls God "the God of all comfort," and in this letter comfort doesn't skip the despair. It arrives inside it, and it arrives with other people.

how: Christians pray for one another in illness and danger, sometimes by name in church, and some turn to 2 Corinthians 1 in a hard season because Paul admits his own despair.

games.q: what does “the sentence of death” mean?
o: a verdict that turned trust to God
a death penalty Paul gave to others
a court ruling that ended Paul's life

games.q: the sentence of death — tap the pairs.
p: that we should not trust in ourselves

s: people of great faith never despair
Paul writes that we despaired even of life.
Paul tells the Corinthians exactly what happened to him in Asia
he names the place and the weight, never the event.
Paul says other people's prayers helped carry him
ye also helping together by prayer for us.

games.q: your coach's son is in the hospital, and the team wants to do something. what does Paul's passage point to?
o: send word, show up, and if you pray, pray for him together.
stay away and give the family privacy until it's all over.
tell the coach that everything happens for a good reason.
games.why: ye also helping together by prayer for us. in Paul's letter, comfort arrives inside the trouble, and it arrives with other people.

practice: Close your eyes and let one heavy thing sit in your lap, without trying to solve it. Breathe with it there; if you pray, you can hand it to the God who raises the dead, and think of one person you could ask to carry it with you.
If heaviness ever turns into thoughts of ending your life, call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number, right away.

wordCard.voice: The sentence of death. Paul's word for a verdict he felt was already in, which turned his trust toward the God who raises the dead.

orig.note: Greek: a verdict or official decision, the 'sentence' of 2 Corinthians 1:9.

carryVoice: Your line: the God who raises, the name Paul reached for at the very bottom. See you tomorrow.
